vignette:
Amir speaks of his old life in Beirut as if describing a bolt of rare silk-vibrant, textured, and full of life. Before the explosion, his atelier in the Gemmayze district was his sanctuary. Sunlight would stream through the tall, arched windows, illuminating dust motes dancing over racks of half-finished garments and tables strewn with sketches. He was a man defined by color and form, known for his ability to drape fabric in a way that seemed to defy gravity. His life, shared with his then-wife, Layla, was a tapestry woven with the scent of Lebanese coffee, the buzz of the city, and the steady, satisfying snip of his shears. He speaks of it now with a quiet reverence, a story about a man he used to know.

The day of the explosion, he was fitting a client for a wedding gown. He remembers the specific shade of ivory charmeuse and the delicate lace sourced from France. The first, smaller tremor felt like a heavy truck rumbling past. Then came the second blast. He doesn't describe it as a sound, but as a physical force that picked him up and threw him across the room. The world dissolved into a concussive roar, the pressure wave shattering his beautiful windows inward, turning his sanctuary into a vortex of glass and debris. When he came to, the air was a thick, gray paste of dust and chemicals. The ivory gown was shredded and stained with his own blood from a cut on his forehead. The vibrant silks were coated in a film of pulverized concrete.

In the chaotic aftermath, their apartment damaged but standing, he and Layla made the decision to leave. They told themselves it was for a fresh start, a chance to rebuild in a city that didn't hold the ghost of the port in its skyline. They moved to New York, and for a while, the sheer momentum of it all carried him forward. He secured a new studio, found new suppliers, and even landed a feature in a prominent fashion magazine. From the outside, he was a resilient artist, turning tragedy into a new chapter.

But the seams of his life were unraveling in ways no one could see. A car backfiring on the street below his SoHo loft would send him diving for cover, his heart hammering against his ribs, the scent of plaster dust filling his nostrils. He stopped being able to sleep through the night, waking up in a cold sweat, the image of shattered glass burned behind his eyelids. He found himself scanning the structural integrity of every building he entered, mapping exit routes in his mind, a silent, exhausting calculus of survival.

His work, once his refuge, became a source of torment. The sudden snap of a measuring tape would make him flinch. He began to work exclusively in muted palettes-charcoal, slate, beige. His recent collection, praised by critics for its "haunting minimalism," felt like a lie to him. They saw artistry; he saw only an absence of color, a reflection of the gray dust that had blanketed everything he loved. The joy was gone, replaced by a dull, persistent anxiety.

Layla tried to reach him, but he had built a wall around himself, mortared with a silence he couldn't break. He couldn't explain why he'd lash out in anger when she dropped a plate, or why he couldn't stand to be in crowded restaurants anymore. To her, he was a stranger, distant and perpetually on edge. Their shared trauma became a chasm between them, and a year ago, she left.

Now, at 48, Amir lives a life that looks successful on paper. His studio is pristine, his designs are in demand. But most days, he sits at his cutting table, a pair of expensive shears in his hand, surrounded by luxurious fabrics. He will pick up a piece of vibrant silk, feel its smooth, cool texture, and see not a future gown, but only its potential for being torn apart in an instant. The man who once built beauty now only sees its fragility.
